definition: Raising a subject by claiming you will not mention it.
exampleSentence: By apophasis he reminded everyone of the scandal: "I won't dwell on his bankruptcy."
etymology: From Greek 'apophanai' (to say no), via Late Latin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An abrupt shift to a different grammatical construction within one sentence.
exampleSentence: His speech dissolved into anacoluthon - "I really ought to, well, do as you like."
etymology: From Greek 'anakolouthos' (inconsistent); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repeating the last word of a clause at the start of the next.
exampleSentence: "Fear leads to anger; anger leads to hate" is a textbook anadiplosis.
etymology: From Greek 'anadiplosis' (a doubling back); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Immediate, emphatic repetition of a word for emphasis.
exampleSentence: "Never, never, never give up" is epizeuxis at its most rousing.
etymology: From Greek 'epizeuxis' (a fastening upon); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repeating the same word at the end of successive clauses.
exampleSentence: "Of the people, by the people, for the people" closes each phrase with epistrophe.
etymology: From Greek 'epistrophe' (a turning about); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Omitting conjunctions between a series of related clauses.
exampleSentence: "I came, I saw, I conquered" gains its speed from asyndeton.
etymology: From Greek 'asyndetos' (unconnected); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Deliberate use of many conjunctions in close succession.
exampleSentence: "We have ships and men and money and stores" piles on polysyndeton.
etymology: From Greek 'poly' (many) + 'syndeton' (bound together); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repetition of words in successive clauses in reverse order.
exampleSentence: "Eat to live, not live to eat" is a crisp antimetabole.
etymology: From Greek 'antimetabole' (turning about); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sentence whose surprise ending reframes its earlier part.
exampleSentence: "I want to die peacefully like my grandfather, not screaming like his passengers" is pure paraprosdokian.
etymology: From Greek 'para' (contrary to) + 'prosdokia' (expectation); a headword in Dictionary.com.

definition: Repeating the opening word of a clause at its end.
exampleSentence: "The king is dead, long live the king" frames itself with epanalepsis.
etymology: From Greek 'epanalepsis' (a taking up again); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Posing a question then immediately answering it yourself.
exampleSentence: She used hypophora: "What should we do? We should begin at once."
etymology: From Greek 'hypophora' (a carrying under); a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: An inverted parallelism in which terms are reversed across clauses.
exampleSentence: "Ask not what your country can do for you" is a famous chiasmus.
etymology: From Greek 'chiasmos' (a crossing), after the letter chi; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repetition of a word at the beginning of successive clauses.
exampleSentence: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds" rides on anaphora.
etymology: From Greek 'anaphora' (a carrying back); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Expressing one idea with two words linked by 'and'.
exampleSentence: "Nice and warm" is hendiadys for "nicely warm."
etymology: From Greek 'hen dia dyoin' (one through two); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A double reading or twofold interpretation of a text.
exampleSentence: The verse invites dittology, supporting two equally valid readings.
etymology: From Greek 'dittos' (double) + '-logia'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A harsh or blunt term used in place of a milder one.
exampleSentence: Calling a graveyard a "bone yard" is a grim dysphemism.
etymology: From Greek 'dys' (bad) + 'pheme' (speech); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Understatement that affirms something by negating its contrary.
exampleSentence: Saying "she's not bad at chess" about a champion is sly litotes.
etymology: From Greek 'litotes' (plainness), from 'litos' (simple); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Rhetorical understatement that belittles something to make a point.
exampleSentence: Calling a hurricane "a spot of weather" is wry meiosis.
etymology: From Greek 'meiosis' (a lessening); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: One word governing two others in different senses simultaneously.
exampleSentence: "She broke his car and his heart" turns on a neat syllepsis.
etymology: From Greek 'syllepsis' (a taking together); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Joy felt at a loved one's happiness in another relationship.
exampleSentence: Watching her partner laugh with his girlfriend, she felt genuine compersion, not jealousy.
etymology: Coined on 28 November 1980 by the Kerista Commune via an alphabet board; a headword in Dictionary.com, which dates first use to 1990-95.

definition: The joyful anticipation that comes from imagining a future pleasure.
exampleSentence: Booking the trip filled her with months of delicious vorfreude.
etymology: German 'vor' (before) + 'Freude' (joy); a documented loanword explored in The Guardian's 9 April 2024 feature on anticipatory joy.

definition: An intense, wistful yearning for something undefined or unattainable.
exampleSentence: The old photograph stirred a deep sehnsucht for a home that no longer existed.
etymology: German 'Sehnen' (yearning) + 'Sucht' (craving); a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune.
exampleSentence: He watched his rival's downfall with undisguised epicaricacy.
etymology: From Greek 'epi' (upon) + 'chara' (joy) + 'kakon' (evil); recorded as 'epicharikaky' in Nathan Bailey's 1721 Universal Etymological English Dictionary.

definition: Intense, almost overwhelming pleasure or enjoyment.
exampleSentence: There was a reckless jouissance in the way she danced until dawn.
etymology: French 'jouir' (to enjoy), from Latin 'gaudere'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Sorrow, grief, or deep anguish.
exampleSentence: A quiet dolor settled over the house in the weeks after the funeral.
etymology: From Latin 'dolor' (pain, grief); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The overwhelming urge to squeeze something unbearably cute.
exampleSentence: Seeing the puppy's fat little paws, she was seized by gigil.
etymology: From Tagalog 'gigil'; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in its March 2025 update, with English usage dated to 1990.

definition: Anxiety that time is running out to act before opportunities close.
exampleSentence: A wave of torschlusspanik hit him at forty, certain his chances were vanishing.
etymology: German 'Tor' (gate) + 'Schluss' (closing) + 'Panik' (panic); a documented loanword used as the title of a Time Magazine article on 18 August 1961.

definition: Vicarious joy taken in the happiness or success of others.
exampleSentence: Cheering his teammate's win, he felt only mudita, never envy.
etymology: From Pali and Sanskrit 'mudita' (gladness); a documented loanword in English-language Buddhist writing.

definition: Careful, appreciative tasting of food or wine in small portions.
exampleSentence: The restaurant's degustation moved through nine small, exquisite courses.
etymology: From Latin 'degustare' (to taste); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The quality in a substance that produces a sensation of taste.
exampleSentence: The broth had a deep, savory sapor that lingered on the tongue.
etymology: From Latin 'sapor' (taste, flavor); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Food or nourishment; that which sustains.
exampleSentence: Bread and olives were the simple aliment of the mountain village.
etymology: From Latin 'alimentum' (nourishment), from 'alere' (to nourish); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A rich Spanish stew of meats and vegetables; any miscellaneous mixture.
exampleSentence: The anthology was a delightful olla podrida of essays, poems, and recipes.
etymology: Spanish for 'rotten pot', 'olla' (pot) + 'podrida' (rotten); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sweet dessert of milk curdled with rennet.
exampleSentence: For pudding there was a wobbling junket dusted with nutmeg.
etymology: From Old French 'jonquette', from Latin 'juncus' (reed basket); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To soften a painting's colors or lines with a thin opaque, dry-brush layer.
exampleSentence: Turner would scumble pale clouds over a darker sky to evoke sea mist.
etymology: Probably a frequentative of 'scum' (to skim); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An opaque watercolor paint, or a painting made with it.
exampleSentence: She rendered the poster in flat, vivid fields of gouache.
etymology: French, from Italian 'guazzo' (watercolor); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A small preliminary model for a sculpture or larger work.
exampleSentence: The sculptor shaped a clay maquette before casting the monument.
etymology: French, from Italian 'macchietta' (little sketch); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A design cut into a surface, the reverse of relief.
exampleSentence: The signet ring bore a tiny intaglio of a leaping stag.
etymology: Italian, from 'intagliare' (to engrave); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The green or bluish coating that forms on weathered copper or bronze.
exampleSentence: Centuries of rain had cloaked the statue in soft verdigris.
etymology: From Old French 'vert-de-Grece' (green of Greece); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An art technique of rubbing to transfer the texture of a surface.
exampleSentence: Max Ernst pioneered frottage, rubbing pencil over grained floorboards.
etymology: French, from 'frotter' (to rub); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A red mercury-sulfide mineral, source of the vermilion pigment.
exampleSentence: The lacquer box glowed a deep cinnabar red.
etymology: From Greek 'kinnabari', of Eastern origin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A white plaster ground prepared on a surface before painting.
exampleSentence: She brushed three coats of gesso onto the panel before sketching.
etymology: Italian, from Latin 'gypsum'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The bristling of body hair from cold, fear, or excitement; goose bumps.
exampleSentence: The choir's final chord sent a wave of horripilation down her arms.
etymology: From Late Latin 'horripilatio', from 'horrere' (to bristle) + 'pilus' (hair); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fleshy strip of tissue dividing the nostrils.
exampleSentence: The piercing passed neatly through her columella.
etymology: From Latin 'columella' (little column); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The small cartilage flap in front of the ear canal.
exampleSentence: He pressed the tragus to muffle the ringing in his ear.
etymology: From Greek 'tragos' (he-goat), for its tuft of hair; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The armpit.
exampleSentence: The nurse placed the thermometer in the patient's axilla.
etymology: From Latin 'axilla' (armpit); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A small fold of tissue that restrains an organ's movement.
exampleSentence: The fold of skin beneath the tongue is the lingual frenulum.
etymology: From Latin 'frenulum' (little bridle); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Relating to the hollow at the back of the knee.
exampleSentence: The doctor checked the pulse in the popliteal artery behind his knee.
etymology: From Latin 'poples' (back of the knee); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fleshy mound of the palm at the base of the thumb.
exampleSentence: She massaged the aching thenar after a long day of typing.
etymology: From Greek 'thenar' (palm of the hand); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The eighth power of a number, in obsolete mathematical notation.
exampleSentence: In Recorde's notation, the zenzizenzizenzic of two is two hundred fifty-six.
etymology: Coined by Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in his 1557 'The Whetstone of Witte'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary, which holds only this single citation.

definition: The slow apparent wobble of the moon seen from Earth.
exampleSentence: Thanks to libration, we can glimpse a little past the moon's near side.
etymology: From Latin 'libratio' (a balancing), from 'libra' (scales); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The point in an orbit nearest the sun.
exampleSentence: The comet blazed brightest as it swept through perihelion.
etymology: From Greek 'peri' (near) + 'helios' (sun); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The point in an orbit farthest from the sun.
exampleSentence: At aphelion the planet slows, drifting at its greatest distance from the sun.
etymology: From Greek 'apo' (away from) + 'helios' (sun); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A blossoming; also a powdery crystalline crust forming on a surface.
exampleSentence: A white efflorescence of salt bloomed across the damp brick wall.
etymology: From Latin 'efflorescere' (to blossom), from 'flos' (flower); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A point of greatest or least distance in an orbit.
exampleSentence: Each apsis marks where the satellite is nearest to or farthest from Earth.
etymology: From Greek 'hapsis' (arch, loop); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The property of a gel turning fluid when shaken and resetting at rest.
exampleSentence: The paint's thixotropy lets it flow under the brush yet not drip on the wall.
etymology: From Greek 'thixis' (touch) + 'trope' (turning); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fully shadowed inner region of a shadow, as in an eclipse.
exampleSentence: Only within the moon's umbra does the sun vanish completely.
etymology: From Latin 'umbra' (shadow); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A table giving the calculated positions of a celestial body over time.
exampleSentence: The navigator consulted an ephemeris to fix the ship's position by the stars.
etymology: From Greek 'ephemeros' (lasting a day); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The unknowing fabrication of false memories without intent to deceive.
exampleSentence: His vivid account was pure confabulation, stitched from gaps in his memory.
etymology: From Latin 'confabulari' (to talk together); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A dissociative state of amnesia in which one wanders from home or identity.
exampleSentence: He emerged from the fugue days later in another city, with no memory of leaving.
etymology: From Latin 'fuga' (flight); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially constructive activity.
exampleSentence: Through sublimation he poured his restless anger into long-distance running.
etymology: From Latin 'sublimare' (to elevate); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The release of emotional tension by reliving a repressed experience.
exampleSentence: The session triggered a sudden abreaction, and years of grief poured out.
etymology: From Latin 'ab-' (away) + 'reaction', translating German 'Abreagieren'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The Swedish principle of 'just the right amount'; balanced moderation.
exampleSentence: Their home embodied lagom: enough comfort, nothing excessive.
etymology: Swedish 'lagom' (just right); a headword in Dictionary.com.

definition: Love of strangers; warm, generous hospitality toward guests.
exampleSentence: The villagers' philoxenia meant no traveler ever went unfed.
etymology: From Greek 'philos' (loving) + 'xenos' (stranger); a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A code of silence and refusal to cooperate with authorities.
exampleSentence: The whole neighborhood maintained an unbreakable omerta about the crime.
etymology: Sicilian Italian 'omerta', perhaps from Spanish 'hombredad' (manliness); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The belief in a shared humanity binding all people: 'I am because we are'.
exampleSentence: Her leadership was rooted in ubuntu, treating every worker as part of one family.
etymology: From Nguni Bantu 'ubuntu' (humanity); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: One's friends and acquaintances, as distinct from kin.
exampleSentence: He returned to the village to be among his kith and kin once more.
etymology: From Old English 'cyththu' (kinsfolk), from 'cunnan' (to know); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Cozy, convivial, and pleasantly sociable.
exampleSentence: The candlelit cafe felt wonderfully gezellig on a rainy night.
etymology: Dutch, from 'gezel' (companion); a documented loanword in English-language media, listed in the Cambridge Dutch-English Dictionary.

definition: The science and art of measuring time and making timepieces.
exampleSentence: His passion for horology filled the shelves with antique clocks.
etymology: From Greek 'hora' (hour) + '-logia' (study); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or relating to a leap year or its extra day.
exampleSentence: February gains a day in every bissextile year.
etymology: From Latin 'bisextilis', from 'bis' (twice) + 'sextus' (sixth); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Weekly; occurring once every seven days.
exampleSentence: The society held its hebdomadal meeting every Thursday evening.
etymology: From Greek 'hebdomas' (seven, a week), from 'hepta' (seven); a headword in Merriam-Webster.
